title: Global Warming
question: How is the Earth’s climate changing, what role do people play, and what should the country do about it?
summary: The measurements of carbon dioxide and temperature, kept separate from the argument over how much harm is coming and what the rules should be.
sourceNote: This page is an original short explanation for students. It is not a copy of Just Facts, and it is not legal, tax, or investment advice. Figures and charts were checked against the sources below on November 21, 2026. A chart uses every year in its data file. Axes include zero when the number is a count, a concentration, or an area, and they include the zero line when the number is a change from an average. Just Facts has a much longer research page, linked below, for further reading. A chart that would compare climate-model output with satellite temperatures was not drawn: this page only charts a data file it downloaded, and that comparison needs a full set of model runs for one layer of the air.

charts.title: Carbon dioxide in the air at Mauna Loa
charts.shows: The yearly average amount of carbon dioxide in dry air at Mauna Loa, Hawaii. It was 315.98 parts per million in 1959 and 427.35 in 2025. The vertical axis starts at zero. The early years in NOAA’s file were measured by C. David Keeling at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography.
charts.doesNotShow: Temperature, storms, or harvests. A higher amount of this gas is a measurement, not by itself a measurement of harm.
charts.citedFor: Both sides, as the basic measurement of carbon dioxide in the air. The concern case treats the rise as the main human push on the climate.

charts.title: Global surface temperature, NOAA
charts.shows: How far each year’s average surface temperature was from the 1901–2000 average, in degrees Celsius. The number for a year is the average of that year’s twelve monthly values in NOAA’s file. 2024 is the warmest year in the file, about 1.26°C above the baseline. 2025 is the third warmest, about 1.12°C above it. The zero line is the 1901–2000 average.
charts.doesNotShow: The temperature of one city, or the temperature in 2100. Another agency can print a different degree number if it chooses a different baseline. This chart is not a forecast.
charts.citedFor: The concern case: the planet’s surface has warmed, and the warmest years are the recent ones.
charts.sourceName: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, Climate at a Glance

charts.title: Global sea level from satellites
charts.shows: The yearly average of NOAA’s satellite sea-level record, in millimeters, from 1993 through 2024. The 2024 average is 103 millimeters, about 10 centimeters, higher than the 1993 average. NOAA’s file also states a straight-line rise of 3.17 millimeters per year, and says that fit does not include a correction for the slow rebound of the Earth’s crust. The zero line is the center of this satellite record, not the sea level of 1900.
charts.doesNotShow: Sea level before satellites, or the change at one beach. A global average can rise while one coast does something different. 2025 is left out because the downloaded file stops in February 2025.
charts.citedFor: The concern case: measured sea level has risen during the satellite era.

charts.title: September Arctic sea ice
charts.shows: How much ocean in the Arctic was covered by at least 15 percent ice in September, when the ice is usually at its smallest. 1979 was 7.05 million square kilometers. September 2026 was 4.81. The lowest September in this file is 2012, at 3.57. The vertical axis starts at zero.
charts.doesNotShow: Ice thickness, ice in other months, or a drop in every single year. The line goes down from the start of the record, and it also goes up in some years.
charts.citedFor: The concern case: late-summer Arctic ice covers less ocean than it did when satellites began watching it.
charts.sourceName: NOAA and the National Snow and Ice Data Center, Sea Ice Index

charts.title: Surface temperature and the satellite record
charts.shows: Two measurements from 1979 through 2025, shifted so each line’s own 1991–2020 average sits on zero. The solid line is NOAA’s surface average. The dashed line is the University of Alabama in Huntsville satellite record for the lower atmosphere, kept by Roy Spencer and John Christy. A straight line through the yearly NOAA numbers rises about 0.20°C per decade. The same kind of line through the satellite numbers rises about 0.16°C per decade. The satellite file itself prints 0.16°C per decade for its global column. Shifting the baselines does not change those rises.
charts.doesNotShow: Whether a climate model is right or wrong. The two lines measure different layers of the air. The chart also leaves out 2026, because the satellite file did not yet have all twelve months.
charts.citedFor: The cost-of-policy case: the lower atmosphere has warmed too, and its rise in this period is a bit slower than the surface record. Both lines go up.
charts.sourceName: NOAA Climate at a Glance and the University of Alabama in Huntsville

charts.title: Reported deaths from weather and climate disasters
charts.shows: The average number of reported deaths per year, by decade, from droughts, floods, storms, wildfires, and extreme heat and cold. Earthquakes, volcanoes, and landslides are not included. The 1900s average about 128,000 deaths a year. The 2010s average about 18,000. The last bar is only 2020 through 2025, six years, and it averages about 46,000, higher than the 2010s. The single highest year in the file is 1931, at about 3.7 million. The axis starts at zero.
charts.doesNotShow: That dangerous weather has become rare. Deaths can fall because of warnings, food aid, medicine, and stronger buildings even if the weather gets harsher. A few huge famines dominate the early decades. EM-DAT counts confirmed deaths plus missing people.
charts.citedFor: The cost-of-policy case: the human toll counted in this record is much lower than it was a century ago, even though the world has more people.
charts.sourceName: EM-DAT, CRED / UCLouvain, processed by Our World in Data

charts.title: Weather disaster losses as a share of the world economy
charts.shows: Worldwide weather and climate disaster losses divided by world GDP, each year from 1990 through 2017. The loss numbers are Munich Re’s, published by Roger Pielke Jr. in 2018. They bounce between 0.10% and 0.48% of world GDP. The highest year in the file is 2005, at 0.48%. The last year, 2017, is 0.40%. The axis starts at zero.
charts.doesNotShow: Any year after 2017. It also does not show how many storms happened, or how many people died. Dollar damage can grow because people build more valuable things in the path of storms. Dividing by GDP is one way to account for a bigger economy.
charts.citedFor: The cost-of-policy case: over these years, losses did not take a steadily larger share of the world economy.
charts.sourceName: Pielke (2018), using Munich Re, processed by Our World in Data

charts.title: World cereal harvest per hectare
charts.shows: Tonnes of cereal grain harvested per hectare, worldwide, from 1.35 in 1961 to 4.21 in 2024. The axis starts at zero.
charts.doesNotShow: Why the harvest rose. Better seeds, fertilizer, and irrigation did much of that work. The chart also does not show how many people are hungry, and it does not separate any help from extra carbon dioxide.
charts.citedFor: The cost-of-policy case: global crop yields have risen a lot during the same decades the air gained carbon dioxide and the surface warmed.
charts.sourceName: Food and Agriculture Organization, compiled by Our World in Data

paragraphs: Global warming means the Earth’s average temperature rising over many years. It is not the same thing as one hot afternoon, or one cold winter.

Sunlight warms the Earth. Some of that heat goes back to space. Gases in the air, including carbon dioxide, methane, and water vapor, hold some of the heat in. That is the greenhouse effect. It is part of why the planet is warm enough to live on. The argument is about the extra greenhouse gas people add, mostly by burning coal, oil, and natural gas, and by clearing forests.

Carbon dioxide is counted in parts per million: how many molecules of the gas are in a million molecules of dry air. At Mauna Loa, in Hawaii, the yearly average was about 316 parts per million in 1959 and about 427 in 2025.
after: A temperature number needs a baseline, the set of years a scientist calls normal. Two groups can agree on the warming and still print different degree numbers, because they picked different normals. This page labels every baseline.
bullets: The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, in its 2023 summary of the science, says human activities, mainly greenhouse-gas emissions, have unequivocally caused global warming. Global surface temperature in 2011–2020 was 1.09°C above 1850–1900. The very likely range around that figure is 0.95°C to 1.20°C.

For the years from 1850–1900 to 2010–2019, the same summary’s best estimate of the human-caused warming is 1.07°C. Natural drivers, the sun and volcanoes, changed global temperature by about −0.1°C to +0.1°C. Well-mixed greenhouse gases likely warmed the surface by 1.0°C to 2.0°C. Other human effects, mainly tiny particles called aerosols, likely cooled it by 0°C to 0.8°C.
Those sentences are about the past. They are not a forecast of the year 2100.

paragraphs: The amount of carbon dioxide in the air, and the rise in the measured temperature, are not the main fight. The fight is about two questions that often get mashed together: how much harm further warming will do, and what governments should require people and companies to do.

Future warming depends on how much greenhouse gas people add, and on how sensitive the climate is to that gas. Equilibrium climate sensitivity is the warming scientists expect, eventually, if the amount of carbon dioxide in the air doubles. The IPCC’s 2021 science report gives a best estimate of 3°C, a likely range of 2.5°C to 4°C, and a very likely range of 2°C to 5°C. A wide range means the same emissions can lead to different amounts of warming.

The IPCC also publishes projections. A projection is a careful estimate, not a record of something that has already happened. Compared with 1850–1900, the average temperature for 2081–2100 is very likely to be 1.0°C to 1.8°C on a very low emissions path, 2.1°C to 3.5°C on a middle path, and 3.3°C to 5.7°C on a very high path. In every path they studied, warming continues until at least the middle of the century unless emissions fall deeply.

One side hears those ranges and says the high end is a reason to cut emissions now. The other side hears the same ranges and says a law should not be written as if the hottest path were already a fact, because changing the energy system has a cost.

sides.intro: Each column is the strongest fair case for that view. The charts in a column are ones that view usually cites. They are drawn from data files downloaded for this page. Read the lines under a chart: what it shows, and what it does not show.

a.title: Cut emissions, because the risk grows with the heat
paragraphs: This side starts with the measurements. The surface record rises, and the warmest years are the recent ones. Sea level measured by satellites is higher than it was in the 1990s. Late-summer Arctic ice covers less ocean than it did when those satellites began.
after: The IPCC says human-caused climate change is already affecting many weather and climate extremes in every region. Since the 1950s, heavy rain has become more frequent and more intense over most land where the records are good enough to judge, and human influence is likely the main driver. With each additional bit of warming, hot extremes and heavy rain get more intense. Global sea level has risen faster since 1900 than in any century in at least the last 3,000 years, the IPCC says, with high confidence. In 2011–2020, late-summer Arctic sea ice area was smaller than at any time in at least the past 1,000 years, with medium confidence.

On the charts above, September Arctic ice was 7.05 million square kilometers in 1979 and 4.81 in 2026. The lowest September in the file is 2012, at 3.57, so the ice has not fallen in a straight line. It is still far below the start of the record. From the 1993 satellite average to the 2024 average, global sea level on NOAA’s record rose 103 millimeters, about 10 centimeters.

This side says waiting makes the later cuts steeper if the world still wants one of the lower paths. It also says people who did the least to cause the emissions are often the most exposed to the heat, the rain, and the water.

The honest version of this view does not pretend that energy can be swapped out for free, or that one country’s law sets the whole world’s temperature. It says the cost of landing on a high warming path is the bigger risk, so it is worth paying to cut emissions now and to get ready for heat, floods, and higher seas.

b.title: Count the warming, and weigh the cost of the rules
paragraphs: This side does not have to deny the thermometer. The satellite record of the lower atmosphere rises too. From 1979 through 2025 it rises a bit more slowly than NOAA’s surface record. The two instruments are not looking at the same layer of air.
after: The IPCC’s own report says there is low confidence in long-term trends in the number of tropical cyclones of all strengths. It also says the share of major cyclones, category 3 to 5, has likely increased over about forty years. Drought is regional: human influence has contributed to more agricultural and ecological drought in some regions, and the report does not describe one worldwide drought trend of a single kind. A hotter planet is not the same sentence as “every kind of storm has become more common.”

Reported deaths from droughts, floods, storms, wildfires, and extreme temperatures are far below the famine decades of the early 1900s. They are not a straight slide, though. The 2020–2025 average is higher than the 2010s. Weather-disaster losses as a share of the world economy, in Roger Pielke Jr.’s 2018 series from Munich Re data, bounce between 0.10% and 0.48% of GDP from 1990 through 2017. They do not climb in a straight line, and the file stops in 2017.

World cereal yields rose from 1.35 tonnes per hectare in 1961 to 4.21 in 2024. A 2016 satellite study led by Zaichun Zhu, and described by NASA, found that from a quarter to a half of Earth’s vegetated land greened between 1982 and 2015. The researchers attributed about 70% of that greening to extra carbon dioxide and about 9% to nitrogen. They also said plants can adjust so the fertilizer effect fades, and that carbon dioxide still traps heat. This page does not chart that study, because the public write-up is a map and a set of shares, not a yearly table this site downloaded.

In 2024, fossil fuels were 82% of the energy used in the United States: petroleum 38%, natural gas 36%, and coal 8%. In 2022, U.S. energy-related carbon dioxide from fossil fuels was 4,941 million metric tons, out of a world total of 38,502 million in the same table, about 13%. A U.S. rule does not, by itself, set the world’s temperature.

The honest version of this view agrees that the air has more carbon dioxide, that the Earth has warmed, and that the IPCC finds people to be the main cause. The argument is that harm has to be counted in lives and costs, not only in degrees, and that replacing most of an energy system has a price. Money spent as if the hottest projection were already certain cannot also be spent on warnings, stronger buildings, or research.

paragraphs: Both sides can use the same measurements. Carbon dioxide in the air is higher than it was in 1959. The surface and the lower atmosphere are both warmer than they were in 1979. A baseline has to be named, or two true temperature numbers look like a quarrel.
bullets: Projections are not promises. The IPCC’s very likely range for climate sensitivity, 2°C to 5°C, is wide on purpose.
A death toll and a temperature are different measurements. Fewer reported deaths do not erase the warming. The warming does not, by itself, tell you how many people will die.
High-confidence findings and low-confidence findings in the same IPCC report both belong in the story. Leaving one of them out changes it.
People need energy they can afford and count on. They also need protection from heat, floods, and higher water.

questions.intro: These questions do not have an answer printed under them.
items: NOAA’s surface record and the satellite record both rise from 1979 to 2025, at about 0.20°C and about 0.16°C per decade. What would you need to know before you said one of them was wrong?
The IPCC’s very likely range for climate sensitivity is 2°C to 5°C. How should a law treat a range that wide?
September Arctic ice was lowest in 2012, not in the latest year, and it is still well below 1979. What can one year prove, and what can it not prove?
Reported deaths from weather and climate disasters are much lower than a century ago, and the 2020–2025 average is higher than the 2010s. What, besides the weather, can change a death toll?

Disaster losses as a share of the world economy did not climb in a straight line from 1990 to 2017, and that file stops in 2017. What would you want to see after 2017 before you updated the conclusion?
Extra carbon dioxide helps plants grow in the 2016 greening study, and it also traps heat. How should that change the way we talk about it?

words.meaning: A gas that holds heat in the atmosphere. Carbon dioxide, methane, and water vapor are greenhouse gases. The planet needs some of this effect. The argument is about the extra gas people add.
A way to count a rare gas. 427 parts per million of carbon dioxide means 427 molecules of that gas in every million molecules of dry air.

The years a temperature number is compared with. NOAA’s surface chart on this page uses 1901–2000. A satellite chart may use 1991–2020. The warming can be the same when the printed degree number is not.
A careful estimate of the future, built from assumptions about emissions and about how the climate responds. It is not a record of what has already happened.
How much the world is expected to warm, eventually, if the amount of carbon dioxide in the air doubles. The IPCC gives a best estimate and a range, not one certain number.
Greenhouse gases released into the air. Burning coal, oil, and natural gas is the largest energy-related source. Clearing forests is another.
